source: Princeton Review APUSH Premium Prep 26E Practice Test 4 (re-conceived; all expression original)

section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: The labor system described above differed from enslaved labor in the colonies most clearly in that it
items.stimulus: In the 1600s, thousands of English men and women signed contracts agreeing to work for a master in Virginia or Maryland for a set number of years. In exchange, the master paid for their voyage across the Atlantic and promised food, clothing, and shelter during the term of service.
options: (A) was organized by churches to convert Native peoples to Christianity
(B) gave workers permanent ownership of the land they farmed
(C) bound workers for a limited term under a signed contract
(D) recruited workers only from the port cities of New England
items.explanation: The workers described are indentured servants. Their defining feature was the contract: they agreed to a fixed term of labor, usually four to seven years, in exchange for passage to America. When the term ended, they were free. Enslaved labor, by contrast, was lifelong and hereditary, with no contract and no set end date.

option_explanations.A: Churches did not organize this labor system. The contracts were commercial agreements between workers and planters or merchants, not religious missions.
option_explanations.B: Servants did not receive land as part of the bargain. Some masters promised clothing or tools at the end of service, but permanent land ownership was not guaranteed.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The signed contract for a limited term is what separated indentured servitude from slavery.
option_explanations.D: Servants came from all over England and other parts of Europe, not only New England ports. Most went to the Chesapeake, not New England.

items.stem: The planters' response to the events described above most directly contributed to which of the following developments?
items.stimulus: In 1676, poor Virginians - Black and white, servant and free - joined Nathaniel Bacon's uprising against the colonial governor. After the rebellion was crushed, Virginia's planter elite changed how they staffed their tobacco fields.
options: (A) the end of tobacco cultivation in Virginia
(B) a lasting political alliance between planters and small farmers
(C) Parliament's decision to outlaw the transatlantic slave trade
(D) the rapid growth of enslaved African labor in the Chesapeake
items.explanation: Many historians argue that Bacon's Rebellion taught Virginia's planters a lesson: a mixed workforce of poor whites and Black laborers could unite against them. In the decades after 1676, planters shifted decisively toward enslaved African laborers, who could be held for life and, under developing slave codes, could never claim the rights of English subjects.

option_explanations.A: Tobacco cultivation did not end. It remained the Chesapeake's main crop, and the shift in labor was meant to keep it profitable.
option_explanations.B: No lasting alliance formed. Planters used the rebellion as a reason to divide poor whites from Black laborers, not to ally with small farmers.
option_explanations.C: Parliament did not outlaw the slave trade until 1807, more than a century later, and the trade actually expanded after Bacon's Rebellion.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The post-1676 shift toward racial slavery is one of the most documented consequences of the rebellion.

items.stem: Compared with the Chesapeake colonies, New England's labor system in the 1700s relied less on bound workers primarily because
options: (A) New England merchants refused to trade with England and the Atlantic world
(B) small family farms and rocky soil made large plantations impractical
(C) the Puritan church forbade all forms of contracted labor in the colonies
(D) New England had no deepwater ports where arriving ships could dock
items.explanation: New England's economy was built on small family farms, fishing, and trade. The rocky soil and short growing season could not support the large tobacco or rice plantations that made bound labor profitable in the Chesapeake and Lower South, so there was far less demand for indentured servants or enslaved workers.

option_explanations.A: New England merchants traded actively with England and the Atlantic world. Trade was central to the region's economy.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Geography and farm size, not law or religion, explain the difference in labor systems.
option_explanations.C: The Puritan church did not forbid contracted labor. Indentured servants did work in New England; there were simply far fewer of them.
option_explanations.D: New England had excellent ports, including Boston. The lack of bound labor had nothing to do with access to shipping.

items.stem: Lincoln's purpose in advancing this argument was most likely to
items.stimulus: "I think the authors of that notable instrument intended to include all men... They meant simply to declare the right, so that the enforcement of it might follow as fast as circumstances should permit." Source: Abraham Lincoln, speech at Alton, Illinois, October 15, 1858.
options: (A) defend the Supreme Court's decision in Dred Scott v. Sandford
(B) argue that the founders meant equality to include Black Americans
(C) demand that Congress abolish slavery immediately
(D) argue that the Declaration of Independence had no real legal importance
items.explanation: Speaking during the Lincoln-Douglas debates, Lincoln used the Declaration to argue that the founders had established equality as a guiding principle that included Black Americans, even though they could not enforce it at once. The argument let him oppose slavery's expansion on moral grounds while stopping short of calling for immediate abolition, the position Illinois voters would have rejected.

option_explanations.A: Lincoln attacked the Dred Scott decision, which had declared that Black people could not be citizens. Defending it would contradict everything in the passage.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The passage's key move is treating equality as a declared right whose enforcement unfolds gradually.
option_explanations.C: Lincoln explicitly rejected immediatism here. He said the founders had 'no power to confer such a boon' at once, which is an argument against immediate abolition.
option_explanations.D: Lincoln treats the Declaration as deeply important, calling it 'that notable instrument' and building his whole case on its meaning.

items.stem: Lincoln's position differed from Garrison's most clearly in its
items.stimulus: In 1831 William Lloyd Garrison began publishing The Liberator, demanding the immediate and unconditional end of slavery. Speaking in 1858, Lincoln argued that the founders had declared equality as a right whose 'enforcement... might follow as fast as circumstances should permit.'
options: (A) the belief that slavery was morally wrong and contradicted American ideals
(B) the demand that Congress prohibit slavery in all western territories
(C) a willingness to accept gradual progress instead of immediate abolition
(D) the call for enslaved people to rise in violent rebellion against slavery
items.explanation: Both men considered slavery wrong, but Garrison demanded immediate abolition as a moral absolute, while Lincoln argued that the founders' promise would be fulfilled gradually as circumstances permitted. That difference between immediatism and gradualism defined the split between abolitionists and the antislavery politicians of the 1850s.

option_explanations.A: Both Lincoln and Garrison believed slavery was morally wrong; they differed on timing and method, not on the moral judgment.
option_explanations.B: Both opposed slavery's expansion. Garrison opposed slavery everywhere, which includes opposing its expansion.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Gradual fulfillment versus immediate abolition is the precise point of disagreement.
option_explanations.D: Neither man supported violence against slaveholders in the passages described. Garrison was a moral-suasion pacifist, and Lincoln worked through politics.

items.stem: Lincoln's argument about the meaning of 'all men are created equal' was made most urgent by which of the following developments?
options: (A) the 1857 Supreme Court ruling that Black people could not be citizens
(B) the admission of California as a free state through the Compromise of 1850
(C) the Missouri Compromise of 1820, which drew a line for slavery
(D) the ratification of the Bill of Rights in 1791
items.explanation: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), the Supreme Court ruled that Black people, free or enslaved, could not be American citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. The decision directly denied that the Declaration's promise applied to Black Americans, which is exactly the claim Lincoln was answering in 1858.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Dred Scott made the meaning of 'all men' a live political question in the year before Lincoln spoke.
option_explanations.B: California's admission was part of the Compromise of 1850 and concerned the balance of free and slave states, not the meaning of the Declaration.
option_explanations.C: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 drew a geographic line for slavery but did not rule on whether Black people were included in 'all men.'
option_explanations.D: The Bill of Rights of 1791 protected individual liberties but did not address the citizenship status of Black Americans.

items.stem: The treaty's promise to bar white settlement most directly reflected which of the following?
items.stimulus: "The United States hereby agrees... that no white person or persons shall be permitted to settle upon or occupy any portion of the same [un-ceded Indian territory]; or without the consent of the Indians... to pass through the same." Source: Treaty of Fort Laramie, Article XVI, 1868.
options: (A) the Sioux desire to adopt American farming methods
(B) a federal plan to build new railroads across Sioux hunting territory in the 1860s
(C) the Sioux decision to leave the Great Plains voluntarily
(D) the military pressure the Sioux had applied during Red Cloud's War
items.explanation: The 1868 treaty followed Red Cloud's War (1866-1868), in which Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces shut down the Bozeman Trail and forced the United States to abandon its forts. The promise to keep white settlers out was a concession the government made because it had lost the fighting, not because of any change of heart.

option_explanations.A: The treaty says nothing about farming. It concerns land rights and the exclusion of settlers, not agricultural methods.
option_explanations.B: No railroad provision appears in Article XVI. The article restricts white movement; it does not authorize construction.
option_explanations.C: The Sioux were not leaving the Plains. The treaty recognized their claim to the territory and tried to keep settlers out of it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Military defeat on the Bozeman Trail is what forced Washington to offer such sweeping terms.

items.stem: The sequence of events described above best illustrates which of the following patterns?
items.stimulus: In 1868 the United States promised the Sioux that no white settlers would enter the Black Hills. In 1874, after gold was found there, thousands of miners rushed in. In 1877 Congress seized the Black Hills outright.
options: (A) the steady expansion of Sioux territory through negotiation
(B) federal courts consistently protecting treaty rights
(C) treaties giving way when settlers demanded Native land
(D) Native nations initiating the renegotiation of treaties
items.explanation: The pattern repeated across the West: treaties recognized Native land rights until settlers or miners wanted the land, at which point the government broke or rewrote the agreement. The Black Hills sequence - promise, gold rush, seizure - is one of the clearest examples.

option_explanations.A: Sioux territory shrank, not expanded; the 1877 act took the Black Hills away.
option_explanations.B: Courts did not protect these treaty rights at the time. The Supreme Court later ruled the seizure illegal, in 1980, but did not return the land.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Settler demand for gold overwhelmed the treaty's promises.
option_explanations.D: The Sioux did not initiate renegotiation; miners flooded in illegally and Congress acted to legalize the taking.

items.stem: The discovery of gold in the Black Hills in 1874 most directly led to
options: (A) a lasting peace between the Sioux and the United States
(B) a flood of white miners into Sioux treaty lands
(C) the Sioux selling the Black Hills voluntarily
(D) Congress granting the Sioux new lands in the East
items.explanation: Custer's 1874 expedition confirmed gold in the Black Hills, and newspaper reports set off a rush. Thousands of miners poured into territory the 1868 treaty had reserved to the Sioux, and the army made little effort to stop them.

option_explanations.A: The gold rush led to renewed war, including Little Bighorn in 1876, not peace.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The rush violated the treaty within six years of its signing.
option_explanations.C: The Sioux did not sell; Congress seized the Hills by statute in 1877.
option_explanations.D: Congress took land from the Sioux; it did not grant them eastern lands.

items.stem: The 1934 law marked a reversal of earlier federal Indian policy most directly because it
items.stimulus: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 ended the allotment of reservation land, restored unsold lands to tribal ownership, and allowed tribes to adopt constitutions and manage their own affairs. (Paraphrased from the Act of June 18, 1934.)
options: (A) replaced forced assimilation with tribal self-government
(B) ordered the immediate return of all treaty lands
(C) required Native children to attend distant federal boarding schools
(D) divided reservations into individual family farms for allotment
items.explanation: From the 1880s, federal policy under the Dawes Act tried to dissolve tribes by dividing reservations into individual allotments and sending Native children to boarding schools. The 1934 act, shaped by Commissioner John Collier, reversed course: it ended allotment and encouraged tribal constitutions and self-rule.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Self-government replaced assimilation as the official goal.
option_explanations.B: The act restored some unsold lands but did not return all treaty lands.
option_explanations.C: Boarding schools were part of the earlier assimilation policy, not the 1934 reversal.
option_explanations.D: Dividing reservations into family farms was the Dawes Act's allotment policy, which the 1934 law ended.

items.stem: The cartoon most directly reflects which of the following about the United States in the 1880s?
items.stimulus: [Image: Puck magazine cartoon, 1880, titled 'Welcome to all!' An Uncle Sam figure greets arriving immigrants at the shore.] Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/36/Welcome_to_all%21_LCCN2002719044.jpg (Puck, 1880; public domain via Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress print.)
options: (A) Congress had banned nearly all immigration to the United States by the 1880s
(B) nativist groups had eliminated prejudice against immigrants
(C) business leaders opposed the arrival of immigrant workers
(D) many Americans publicly welcomed immigrants despite nativist opposition
items.explanation: The 1880s were the peak years of the 'new immigration' from southern and eastern Europe. Cartoons like this one celebrated the American tradition of welcome, even as nativist groups such as the American Protective Association organized against Catholic and Jewish immigrants. Both the welcome and the backlash existed at the same time.

option_explanations.A: Congress had not banned nearly all immigration in the 1880s. The only major ban was the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, aimed at one nationality.
option_explanations.B: Nativist groups were active and growing in the 1880s, not eliminated. Prejudice against immigrants remained strong.
option_explanations.C: Business leaders generally favored immigration because it supplied cheap labor for factories, mines, and railroads.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The cartoon captures the pro-immigration side of a national debate that also included organized nativism.

items.stem: The sharp decline in the foreign-born share of the population between 1920 and 1970 was most directly caused by
options: (A) the closing of Ellis Island to immigrants during World War I
(B) the Immigration Act of 1924 and related quota laws
(C) the economic depression of the 1890s
(D) the abolition of slavery in 1865
items.explanation: The Immigration Acts of 1921 and 1924 set strict national-origins quotas that cut immigration, especially from southern and eastern Europe and Asia, to a small fraction of earlier levels. With fewer arrivals and no major new wave until the 1965 reforms, the foreign-born share fell steadily to its low point of 4.7 percent in 1970.

option_explanations.A: Ellis Island remained open through this period; it closed in 1954. The decline was caused by law, not by the station closing.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The quota system of the 1920s is the direct cause of the half-century decline shown in the data.
option_explanations.C: The 1890s depression came before the decline began and cannot explain a drop that started after 1920.
option_explanations.D: The abolition of slavery in 1865 had no direct connection to immigration levels in the 20th century.

items.stem: Nativist movements in the United States in the 1850s and the 1920s were most similar in that both
options: (A) won the presidency for their preferred candidates
(B) focused their hostility on immigrants from Latin America
(C) directed prejudice against Catholic immigrants
(D) succeeded in ending all immigration to the United States
items.explanation: The Know-Nothing movement of the 1850s targeted Irish and German Catholic immigrants, warning that Catholicism threatened American institutions. The revived Ku Klux Klan of the 1920s likewise made Catholics, along with Jews, Black Americans, and immigrants, central targets of its hatred. Anti-Catholic prejudice connects the two movements.

option_explanations.A: Neither movement elected a president. The Know-Nothings ran Millard Fillmore in 1856 and lost; the 1920s Klan never ran its own presidential candidate.
option_explanations.B: Latin American immigration was not a major focus of either movement. The 1850s nativists targeted Irish and Germans; the 1920s nativists targeted southern and eastern Europeans and Asians.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Anti-Catholicism was a core feature of both movements.
option_explanations.D: Neither movement ended immigration. The 1850s movement faded with the Civil War, and the 1920s movement won quotas, not a total ban.

items.stem: After 1965, immigrants to the United States settled in large numbers in the Southwest and the Sun Belt. This pattern is best explained by
options: (A) a federal program that assigned immigrants to western states
(B) job growth in the Sun Belt and proximity to Latin America
(C) the reopening of Ellis Island as an immigration station
(D) the decline of immigration from Asia and Latin America
items.explanation: The Immigration Act of 1965 ended the national-origins quotas, and immigration from Latin America and Asia grew rapidly. Many newcomers settled where jobs were expanding and where communities from their home countries already existed: the Sun Belt's booming economy and the Southwest's closeness to Mexico made those regions natural destinations.

option_explanations.A: No federal program assigned immigrants to particular states. Settlement was driven by jobs and family networks, not government placement.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Economic opportunity plus geographic and community ties explain the regional pattern.
option_explanations.C: Ellis Island closed in 1954 and never reopened as an immigration station.
option_explanations.D: Immigration from Asia and Latin America increased sharply after 1965; it did not decline.

items.stem: McKinley's intended audience for this argument was most likely
items.stimulus: "Under free trade the trader is the master and the producer the slave... 'Buy where you can pay the easiest.' And that spot of earth is where labor wins its highest rewards." Source: William McKinley, speech, 1892.
options: (A) American industrial workers whose wages tariffs were meant to protect
(B) British manufacturers seeking new American markets for their exported goods
(C) Southern farmers who favored free trade in cotton
(D) economists who opposed all tariffs
items.explanation: McKinley's closing line, that protection puts labor where it 'wins its highest rewards,' was pitched to workingmen. The argument was that tariffs shielded American factories from cheap foreign goods, keeping wages high. Republicans used this appeal to win industrial workers' votes in the 1890s.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The speech frames protection as a defense of American labor's wages.
option_explanations.B: British manufacturers wanted free trade to sell into the American market; McKinley was arguing against their interests.
option_explanations.C: Southern farmers generally favored lower tariffs because tariffs raised the prices they paid for manufactured goods.
option_explanations.D: Economists who opposed tariffs would reject McKinley's entire argument rather than be persuaded by it.

items.stem: In the 1890s, opposition to high protective tariffs came most strongly from
options: (A) Northern factory owners protected from foreign competition by tariffs
(B) Republican leaders who championed protective tariffs in every campaign
(C) railroad executives whose businesses depended on industrial growth
(D) Southern and western farmers who paid more for manufactured goods
items.explanation: High tariffs raised the prices of manufactured goods, which hurt the farmers who bought them while doing nothing for the prices farmers received for their crops. Southern and western farmers, organized through the Democratic Party and the Populists, therefore demanded lower tariffs, while Northern manufacturers and Republicans defended protection.

option_explanations.A: Northern factory owners benefited from tariffs, which shielded them from foreign competition.
option_explanations.B: Republican leaders, including McKinley, were the leading champions of high tariffs.
option_explanations.C: Railroad executives were generally aligned with the pro-tariff industrial interests, not with the opposition.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Farmers bore the costs of protection without sharing its benefits, making them the core of the anti-tariff coalition.

items.stem: The high tariffs supported by McKinley most directly benefited
options: (A) American consumers, who paid lower prices for imported goods
(B) American manufacturers, who faced less foreign competition
(C) European exporters to the United States
(D) the federal government's diplomatic relations with trading partners
items.explanation: A protective tariff taxes imported goods, making foreign products more expensive and giving domestic producers room to charge higher prices without being undercut. American manufacturers were the intended and actual beneficiaries of McKinley's tariff policy.

option_explanations.A: Consumers paid higher prices under protective tariffs, since both imported and domestic goods cost more.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Shielding domestic industry from foreign competition was the purpose of protection.
option_explanations.C: European exporters were harmed by tariffs, which made their goods harder to sell in America.
option_explanations.D: Tariffs sometimes strained trade diplomacy rather than improving it.

items.stem: The economic changes described above most directly contributed to
items.stimulus: Between 1800 and 1860, canals, steamboats, and railroads linked American regions into a single commercial web. Northern factories turned to wage labor while Southern plantations expanded cotton production with enslaved labor.
options: (A) a decline in sectional tensions over the future of slavery
(B) sharper economic differences between North and South
(C) the end of cotton production in the Southern states
(D) equal wealth across all regions
items.explanation: The market revolution pulled the sections in opposite directions economically. The North moved toward factories, wage labor, and commercial farming, while the South doubled down on enslaved labor to grow cotton for world markets. As their labor systems diverged, so did their politics, deepening the sectional conflict.

option_explanations.A: Sectional tensions grew worse, not better, as the economies diverged.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Economic divergence between free-labor North and slave-labor South is the key result.
option_explanations.C: Cotton production expanded enormously; it did not end.
option_explanations.D: Wealth remained unevenly distributed between and within regions.

items.stem: The Lowell system best illustrates which of the following changes?
items.stimulus: In the 1820s and 1830s, the textile mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, hired thousands of young women from New England farms. They lived in company boardinghouses and earned cash wages tending power looms.
options: (A) the movement of enslaved labor into Northern factories
(B) the decline of women's participation in the economy
(C) the shift from household production to wage labor
(D) the end of immigration to the United States
items.explanation: Before industrialization, most New England women produced cloth and goods within the household. The Lowell mills moved that work into factories and paid the young women cash wages, creating a new kind of worker: the wage-earning woman living away from home.

option_explanations.A: Northern factories used free wage labor, not enslaved labor.
option_explanations.B: Women's economic participation increased through mill work; it did not decline.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Lowell mills mark the move from household to factory wage labor.
option_explanations.D: Immigration to the United States continued and grew through this period.

items.stem: The completion of the Erie Canal in 1825 most directly
options: (A) made New York City the nation's commercial capital
(B) ended the cultivation of cotton in the Southern states entirely
(C) caused the Panic of 1837 and the depression that followed it
(D) prevented the construction of railroads across the Appalachian Mountains
items.explanation: The canal linked the Great Lakes to the Hudson River and the Atlantic, slashing the cost of moving goods between the West and the East Coast. Trade funneled through New York City, which became the country's dominant commercial center.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The canal's commercial impact centered on New York City.
option_explanations.B: The canal carried western grain and goods; it had no effect on Southern cotton.
option_explanations.C: The Panic of 1837 was caused by banking and land-speculation policies, not the canal.
option_explanations.D: Railroads were built in large numbers after 1825; the canal did not prevent them.

items.stem: Holmes's statement defends which of the following constitutional protections?
items.stimulus: "The best test of truth is the power of the thought to get itself accepted in the competition of the market." Source: Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes, dissenting opinion in Abrams v. United States, 1919.
options: (A) the right to bear arms
(B) freedom of speech
(C) protection against unreasonable searches
(D) the right to a speedy trial
items.explanation: Holmes's 'marketplace of ideas' image is his most famous defense of free speech. He argued that the First Amendment protects even unpopular opinions, because truth emerges from open competition among ideas rather than from government censorship.

option_explanations.A: The right to bear arms is protected by the Second Amendment, which has nothing to do with Holmes's argument about the competition of ideas.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 'competition of the market' is Holmes's metaphor for free public debate, the core of First Amendment speech protection.
option_explanations.C: Protection against unreasonable searches comes from the Fourth Amendment, which concerns privacy and police power, not the exchange of ideas.
option_explanations.D: The right to a speedy trial is a Sixth Amendment criminal-procedure guarantee, unrelated to Holmes's point.

items.stem: Holmes's free-speech dissents of 1919 were most directly written in response to
items.stimulus: During World War I, the federal government prosecuted antiwar speakers under the Espionage Act of 1917 and the Sedition Act of 1918. Socialist leader Eugene Debs was sentenced to ten years in prison for a speech opposing the war.
options: (A) the Palmer Raids against suspected radicals
(B) the Scopes trial over the teaching of evolution
(C) the Ku Klux Klan's march on Washington
(D) the wartime prosecution of antiwar dissenters
items.explanation: Holmes dissented in 1919 cases, including Baltzer v. United States, that upheld convictions of wartime dissenters. His argument that the government should 'err on the side of freedom' was a direct response to the Wilson administration's jailing of critics who opposed American participation in World War I.

option_explanations.A: The Palmer Raids came in late 1919 and 1920, after the dissents, and targeted suspected communists rather than wartime antiwar speakers.
option_explanations.B: The Scopes trial took place in 1925 and concerned the teaching of evolution, not wartime speech.
option_explanations.C: The Klan's 1920s marches were expressions of nativism and racism, not the federal prosecutions Holmes was addressing.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Espionage and Sedition Act prosecutions of 1917-1918 were the immediate context for Holmes's dissents.

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most directly conflicted with Holmes's principle that those in power should 'err on the side of freedom'?
options: (A) the blacklisting of suspected communists in the Second Red Scare
(B) the Supreme Court's protection of criminal suspects' rights in the 1960s
(C) the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(D) the ratification of the 19th Amendment
items.explanation: During the Second Red Scare of the late 1940s and 1950s, loyalty programs, HUAC hearings, and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations cost thousands of Americans their jobs for their political beliefs and associations. Punishing people for their opinions is the opposite of erring on the side of freedom.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Blacklists and loyalty oaths punished speech and association, directly contradicting Holmes's principle.
option_explanations.B: The Warren Court's criminal-procedure rulings expanded individual freedoms, which aligns with Holmes's principle rather than conflicting with it.
option_explanations.C: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 expanded freedom by outlawing segregation and employment discrimination.
option_explanations.D: The 19th Amendment expanded voting rights to women, an expansion of freedom, not a restriction.

items.stem: Dunmore's offer is best understood as
items.stimulus: In November 1775, Lord Dunmore, the royal governor of Virginia, offered freedom to enslaved people held by rebels who would join British forces. (Paraphrased from Dunmore's Proclamation, 1775.)
options: (A) a British plan to abolish slavery throughout the empire after the war
(B) a response to colonial demands for emancipation
(C) a military tactic to weaken the rebellion through slavery
(D) an effort to recruit white colonists away from the rebel cause
items.explanation: Dunmore was losing control of Virginia and needed soldiers. By offering freedom to the enslaved laborers of rebels, he hoped to strip the rebellion of its workforce, frighten slaveholding patriots into submission, and gain Black recruits. The offer was a weapon of war aimed at the South's dependence on slavery, not a humanitarian policy.

option_explanations.A: Britain did not abolish slavery in its empire until 1833, and Dunmore's offer applied only to the enslaved people of rebels, not to slavery generally.
option_explanations.B: Virginia's patriots were not demanding emancipation; most were slaveholders who were outraged by the proclamation.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The proclamation used the threat of slave revolt as military leverage against the rebellion.
option_explanations.D: The offer was directed at enslaved Black people, not white colonists, and it alienated white Virginians rather than recruiting them.

items.stem: Despite the revolutionary ideals of liberty and equality, slavery expanded in the South during the 1700s primarily because
options: (A) the British government required the colonies to import enslaved people
(B) Enlightenment writers persuaded planters to adopt slavery
(C) indentured servants demanded higher wages than planters could pay
(D) profitable plantation crops depended on enslaved labor
items.explanation: Tobacco in the Chesapeake and rice and indigo in the Lower South were highly profitable export crops, and their profits depended on large, controllable workforces. Enslaved labor, which was lifelong and hereditary, gave planters the cheapest and most reliable workforce available. Economic interest overpowered revolutionary ideals.

option_explanations.A: Britain permitted and profited from the slave trade but did not require colonies to import enslaved people; planters chose to buy them.
option_explanations.B: Enlightenment writers generally argued against slavery on the grounds of natural rights; they did not persuade planters to adopt it.
option_explanations.C: Indentured servants became scarcer, but the main driver was the profitability of plantation crops, not servant wage demands.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The plantation economy's demand for profitable, controllable labor is what expanded slavery.

items.stem: The amendment above did which of the following?
items.stimulus: "Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction." Source: 13th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, 1865.
options: (A) granted formerly enslaved men the right to vote in all elections
(B) abolished slavery but left freedpeople's rights undefined
(C) ordered the redistribution of plantation land to freedpeople
(D) guaranteed equal protection under the law
items.explanation: The 13th Amendment ended slavery as an institution but said nothing about what rights formerly enslaved people would hold. That silence left courts and legislatures to argue for years over whether freedpeople could vote, own property, testify, or move freely, a struggle the 14th and 15th Amendments later addressed.

option_explanations.A: Voting rights for Black men came with the 15th Amendment in 1870, not the 13th.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Abolition without a definition of freedpeople's rights is exactly what the text does.
option_explanations.C: The amendment ordered no land redistribution; hopes for 'forty acres' were never written into law.
option_explanations.D: Equal protection is the language of the 14th Amendment (1868), not the 13th.

items.stem: The legal uncertainty about the rights of formerly enslaved people was first addressed at the national level by
options: (A) the Black Codes passed by Southern states to control freedpeople
(B) the Compromise of 1877 that ended Reconstruction
(C) the Supreme Court's decision in Plessy v. Ferguson
(D) the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment
items.explanation: Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1866 to define freedpeople as citizens with rights to contracts, property, and court access, and then wrote those protections into the Constitution with the 14th Amendment's guarantees of citizenship, due process, and equal protection. These were the first national answers to the question the 13th Amendment had left open.

option_explanations.A: The Black Codes restricted freedpeople's rights; they deepened the uncertainty rather than resolving it.
option_explanations.B: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction by withdrawing federal troops; it did not define anyone's rights.
option_explanations.C: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld segregation decades later; it did not address the postwar legal uncertainty.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1866 act and the 14th Amendment were Congress's direct response to the open question of freedpeople's legal status.

items.stem: The developments described above best illustrate
items.stimulus: After 1865, Southern states passed Black Codes restricting the movement and labor of freedpeople. Most freedpeople ended up working as sharecroppers, borrowing supplies at high interest and paying landlords with a share of the crop.
options: (A) the immediate achievement of full economic equality for freedpeople
(B) the success of the Freedmen's Bureau in distributing land to freedpeople
(C) Southern efforts to control Black labor through law and debt
(D) the rapid industrialization of the postwar Southern economy
items.explanation: Black Codes tried to bind freedpeople to plantation labor by law, and when federal pressure weakened the codes, sharecropping and the crop-lien system achieved much the same result through debt. Together they show how white Southerners rebuilt a coerced labor system after slavery's legal end.

option_explanations.A: Freedpeople remained poor and politically vulnerable; equality was not achieved.
option_explanations.B: The Freedmen's Bureau helped with schools and contracts, but its land-redistribution hopes were never realized.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Law and debt replaced slavery as tools of labor control.
option_explanations.D: The postwar South remained overwhelmingly agricultural; industrialization came much later.

items.stem: Eisenhower used this image to justify
items.stimulus: "You have a row of dominoes set up, you knock over the first one, and what will happen to the last one is the certainty that it will go over very quickly." Source: President Dwight D. Eisenhower, press conference, April 7, 1954.
options: (A) American intervention to stop communist takeovers in Southeast Asia
(B) the complete withdrawal of all American troops from the Korean peninsula
(C) negotiations to reduce nuclear weapons
(D) a policy of ignoring political conflicts in developing nations
items.explanation: Eisenhower was explaining why the United States was aiding France in Indochina: if one Southeast Asian nation fell to communism, he argued, its neighbors would follow like dominoes. The domino theory became the central justification for two decades of deepening American involvement in Vietnam.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The domino image was the public case for intervention in Southeast Asia.
option_explanations.B: The Korean War had ended in an armistice the year before; Eisenhower was looking ahead to Southeast Asia, not withdrawing from Korea.
option_explanations.C: The statement concerns communist expansion, not arms control.
option_explanations.D: The domino theory demanded attention to developing nations, not indifference.

items.stem: The domino theory most directly shaped which of the following American actions?
options: (A) the Marshall Plan's aid to Western Europe
(B) the signing of the SALT arms-control treaties
(C) the Cuban Missile Crisis naval quarantine
(D) the escalation of the war in Vietnam
items.explanation: The domino theory held that a communist victory in South Vietnam would topple neighboring states, so presidents from Eisenhower through Nixon treated Vietnam as a test of containment. That logic drove the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution and the buildup to more than half a million American troops.

option_explanations.A: The Marshall Plan (1948) predated the domino theory and aimed at European recovery.
option_explanations.B: SALT concerned nuclear weapons limits with the Soviet Union, not Southeast Asia.
option_explanations.C: The 1962 quarantine addressed Soviet missiles in Cuba, a separate crisis.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Vietnam was the domino theory's main application.

items.stem: One major consequence of the Vietnam War for American foreign policy was
options: (A) a permanent increase in public trust in the presidency after the war
(B) new congressional limits on presidential war powers
(C) the end of all American military alliances
(D) the immediate collapse of the Soviet Union
items.explanation: The long, costly, and ultimately unsuccessful war in Vietnam shattered public confidence and led Congress to pass the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which requires the president to notify Congress and withdraw troops after 60 days without congressional approval. It was a direct legislative response to two decades of presidential escalation in Southeast Asia.

option_explanations.A: Public trust in the presidency declined sharply after Vietnam and Watergate; it did not increase.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The War Powers Resolution was Congress's attempt to reclaim authority over undeclared wars.
option_explanations.C: The United States kept its alliances, including NATO. Vietnam changed how wars were authorized, not whether alliances existed.
option_explanations.D: The Soviet Union did not collapse until 1991, and Vietnam was not its cause.

items.stem: The American war in Vietnam most closely resembled the Korean War in that both
options: (A) ended with a formal American declaration of victory
(B) were fought to support the spread of communism
(C) were undeclared wars fought to contain communism
(D) received unanimous support from the American public
items.explanation: Korea (1950-1953) and Vietnam (1964-1973) were both applications of the containment doctrine in Asia: the United States committed troops without a declaration of war to stop communist forces from taking over a divided country. In both cases the goal was to prevent communist expansion, not to conquer territory.

option_explanations.A: Neither war ended in a declared American victory. Korea ended in an armistice; Vietnam ended with American withdrawal and a communist victory.
option_explanations.B: The United States fought against the spread of communism in both wars, not to support it.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Containment without a declaration of war is the defining similarity.
option_explanations.D: Public support was deeply divided in both wars, especially Vietnam, where opposition grew into a mass movement.

items.stem: In this passage, Washington was urging Black Americans to
items.stimulus: "In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress." Source: Booker T. Washington, Atlanta Compromise speech, 1895.
options: (A) demand immediate voting rights
(B) organize a mass migration of Black families to the North
(C) reject all cooperation with white Southerners entirely
(D) accept social separation while pursuing economic gains
items.explanation: Washington's Atlanta Compromise counseled Black Southerners to accept segregation in social life for the time being and concentrate on economic self-improvement through work, property, and vocational training. The 'fingers' and 'hand' image promised white Southerners that Black workers would be loyal and productive partners in the region's economy.

option_explanations.A: Washington explicitly discouraged agitation for voting rights, calling it 'the extremest folly' in the same speech.
option_explanations.B: Washington opposed mass migration and urged Black Southerners to stay in the South and build up the region's economy.
option_explanations.C: Washington sought cooperation with white Southerners, not rejection of it; the whole speech was an offer of partnership.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Economic progress first, social and political claims later, was the core of Washington's program.

items.stem: Du Bois's position differed from Washington's most clearly in Du Bois's insistence on
items.stimulus: "They are absolutely certain that the way for a people to gain their reasonable rights is [to]... insist continually... that voting is necessary to modern manhood, that color discrimination is barbarism." Source: W. E. B. Du Bois, 'Of Mr. Booker T. Washington and Others,' 1903.
options: (A) direct political agitation for voting rights and equality
(B) the abandonment of all educational efforts
(C) the use of violent rebellion against the federal government
(D) complete separation of the races in all areas of American life
items.explanation: Du Bois rejected Washington's counsel of patience. He argued that Black Americans must openly and continuously demand the vote, civic equality, and higher education, and must condemn discrimination wherever it appeared. Political agitation, not quiet accommodation, was his path to rights.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Insistent public demand for political rights is the heart of Du Bois's criticism of Washington.
option_explanations.B: Du Bois championed education, especially higher education for the 'Talented Tenth' who would lead the race.
option_explanations.C: Du Bois advocated protest and political pressure, not armed rebellion.
option_explanations.D: Du Bois opposed segregation; demanding an end to color discrimination is the opposite of endorsing separation.

items.stem: Despite their well-known disagreement, Washington and Du Bois both believed that
options: (A) segregation laws would never be challenged
(B) the federal government should take no role in advancing Black Americans
(C) violence was the only path to change
(D) Black economic progress through work and education was essential
items.explanation: For all their differences over political strategy, both men placed hard work, property ownership, and education at the center of Black advancement. Washington built Tuskegee around vocational training, and Du Bois, while demanding political rights, also stressed education and economic organization as foundations of progress.

option_explanations.A: Du Bois explicitly called for challenging segregation, and Washington expected discrimination to fade as Black economic power grew.
option_explanations.B: Du Bois wanted federal action against discrimination, and Washington quietly lobbied against segregation laws behind the scenes.
option_explanations.C: Neither man advocated violence; both worked through education, organization, and public argument.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Economic and educational self-improvement was common ground between them.

items.stem: These developments formed the legal backdrop for the Washington-Du Bois debate by
items.stimulus: In the 1890s, Southern states rewrote their constitutions to add poll taxes, literacy tests, and grandfather clauses. In 1896 the Supreme Court upheld segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson.
options: (A) guaranteeing federal protection for Black voters in the South
(B) ending all racial discrimination in the South
(C) making the response to disfranchisement an urgent question
(D) granting Black Southerners full and equal political rights
items.explanation: Washington and Du Bois argued while Southern states were systematically stripping Black men of the vote and the Supreme Court was blessing 'separate but equal.' The debate was not abstract: it was about how Black Americans should respond to a legal counterrevolution that was happening in real time.

option_explanations.A: Federal protection for Black voters had largely ended with Reconstruction; the 1890s moved in the opposite direction.
option_explanations.B: Discrimination was expanding, not ending, through Jim Crow laws and disfranchisement constitutions.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The urgency of disfranchisement is what made the strategic disagreement between the two men matter.
option_explanations.D: Black Southerners were losing political rights in the 1890s, not gaining them.

items.stem: The territory labeled 'Mexican Cession (1848)' was acquired as a direct result of
items.stimulus: Map of United States territorial acquisitions, 1803-1853 (based on Library of Congress maps): Louisiana Purchase (1803), Florida (1819), Texas Annexation (1845), Oregon (1846), Mexican Cession (1848), Gadsden Purchase (1853).
options: (A) a purchase from Spain
(B) the Mexican-American War
(C) a treaty with Great Britain
(D) the annexation of an independent republic by Congress
items.explanation: The United States defeated Mexico in the war of 1846-1848, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo forced Mexico to cede California and the Southwest for $15 million. The acquisition was a conquest formalized by treaty, not a purchase like the Gadsden or a diplomatic settlement like Oregon.

option_explanations.A: Spain sold Florida to the United States in 1819, not the Mexican Cession.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Mexican Cession was the spoils of the Mexican-American War.
option_explanations.C: The treaty with Britain settled the Oregon boundary in 1846; it had nothing to do with the Southwest.
option_explanations.D: Texas was the independent republic annexed by Congress in 1845; the Mexican Cession came three years later through war.

items.stem: O'Sullivan's phrase was intended to
items.stimulus: "Our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence for the free development of our yearly multiplying millions." Source: John L. O'Sullivan, Democratic Review, 1845.
options: (A) justify American expansion across North America
(B) oppose the annexation of Texas by the United States
(C) defend the rights of Native nations to their lands
(D) promote American industrialization
items.explanation: O'Sullivan coined 'manifest destiny' to argue that Providence had assigned North America to the United States. The phrase gave expansionists a moral and religious vocabulary for annexing Texas, taking Oregon, and later seizing the Southwest.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The phrase was a justification for continental expansion.
option_explanations.B: O'Sullivan supported Texas annexation; the essay argued for it.
option_explanations.C: The phrase was used to override Native claims, not defend them.
option_explanations.D: O'Sullivan wrote about territorial expansion, not factories.

items.stem: The Wilmot Proviso was historically significant primarily because it
items.stimulus: In 1846, Congressman David Wilmot proposed banning slavery in any territory acquired from Mexico. The proposal failed in the Senate, but it was reintroduced many times.
options: (A) ended the Mexican-American War in 1848
(B) admitted California as a free state in 1850
(C) created the doctrine of popular sovereignty for new territories
(D) forced slavery's expansion to the center of national politics
items.explanation: The proviso never became law, but it forced every politician to take a position on slavery in the territories. Northern support and Southern fury over the proposal showed that westward expansion had made slavery's future the unavoidable question in American politics.

option_explanations.A: The war ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848, not with the proviso.
option_explanations.B: California entered as a free state under the Compromise of 1850.
option_explanations.C: Popular sovereignty was Stephen Douglas's doctrine, advanced later in the Kansas-Nebraska Act.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The proviso nationalized the slavery-expansion debate.

items.stem: The method of protest Thoreau describes is best known as
items.stimulus: "If a thousand men were not to pay their tax bills this year, that would... be the definition of a peaceable revolution, if any such is possible." Source: Henry David Thoreau, 'Resistance to Civil Government,' 1849.
options: (A) civil disobedience
(B) armed insurrection
(C) judicial review
(D) party realignment
items.explanation: Thoreau argued that individuals should refuse to cooperate with an unjust government, even at the cost of going to jail, as he had done for refusing a poll tax during the Mexican War. Peaceful refusal to obey unjust laws became known as civil disobedience.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Thoreau's essay is the classic American statement of civil disobedience.
option_explanations.B: Thoreau explicitly described a 'peaceable' revolution, not an armed one.
option_explanations.C: Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws, not individual protest.
option_explanations.D: Party realignment concerns shifts in party coalitions, not Thoreau's subject.

items.stem: Thoreau's argument for refusing to obey unjust laws most directly influenced
options: (A) the economic policies of the Reagan administration in the 1980s
(B) the isolationist movement of the 1930s
(C) the nonviolent tactics of the civil rights movement
(D) the expansion of the federal court system
items.explanation: Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience argued that conscience outranks law and that individuals should peacefully refuse to cooperate with injustice. A century later, civil rights leaders including Martin Luther King Jr. cited Thoreau when they chose sit-ins, boycotts, and marches that broke segregation laws without violence.

option_explanations.A: Reagan's economic policies concerned taxes and deregulation, not civil disobedience.
option_explanations.B: The 1930s isolationists wanted to avoid foreign wars; they did not draw on Thoreau's theory of resistance to unjust law.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Nonviolent direct action against segregation was the most direct heir of Thoreau's argument.
option_explanations.D: The federal court system expanded for many reasons, none of them directly tied to Thoreau's essay.

items.stem: The commission's argument for conservation rested on the idea that
items.stimulus: "The only proper basis for the protection of... all animals is an economic one... for the benefit of future generations of our citizens." Source: Massachusetts Commission on Economy and Efficiency, 1912.
options: (A) resources should be managed for long-term human benefit
(B) wildlife had no value to the economy
(C) only state governments, not the federal government, should protect animals
(D) hunting should be banned in all places and circumstances
items.explanation: The commission made a utilitarian case: protecting fish and game was 'wise economy' because it preserved valuable resources for future Americans. This was conservation for human use, not preservation of wilderness for its own sake.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The commission argued that conservation paid off economically over time.
option_explanations.B: The commission argued the opposite: that birds and animals were 'valuable to mankind' and worth protecting for that reason.
option_explanations.C: The commission called for 'properly enforced laws,' a general principle, not a claim that only states should act.
option_explanations.D: The commission favored regulated protection of game, not a total ban on hunting.

items.stem: The commission's economic approach to conservation most closely matched the views of
options: (A) John Muir, who wanted wilderness preserved untouched by commercial use
(B) Andrew Carnegie, who opposed government regulation
(C) William Jennings Bryan, who focused on monetary policy and silver
(D) Gifford Pinchot, who favored scientific management of resources
items.explanation: Gifford Pinchot, the first chief of the U.S. Forest Service under Theodore Roosevelt, argued that natural resources should be managed scientifically for the greatest long-term public benefit. The commission's call for conservation 'for the benefit of future generations' is the same utilitarian philosophy.

option_explanations.A: John Muir was a preservationist who wanted wilderness left untouched by commercial use, the opposite of the commission's economic reasoning.
option_explanations.B: Carnegie favored minimal government interference in business, not state management of natural resources.
option_explanations.C: Bryan's signature issue was the free coinage of silver, not conservation policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Pinchot's 'wise use' conservationism matches the commission's economic argument exactly.

items.stem: Which of the following would NOT support the claim that conservatism was politically marginal during this period?
items.stimulus: In 1964, conservative candidate Barry Goldwater lost the presidency in a landslide. For the next decade and a half, liberal Democrats passed the Great Society programs and held large congressional majorities.
options: (A) Goldwater's overwhelming defeat in 1964
(B) Ronald Reagan's election as president in 1980
(C) the continued expansion of Great Society programs
(D) Democratic dominance of Congress in the 1970s
items.explanation: Goldwater's crushing loss, the growth of liberal programs, and Democratic control of Congress all show conservatism on the sidelines. Reagan's 1980 victory shows the opposite: conservatism had returned to power. It marks the end of the marginal period, so it cannot support the claim that conservatism was marginal.

option_explanations.A: A landslide defeat for the conservative standard-bearer is direct evidence of conservatism's weakness.
option_explanations.B: Correct. A conservative winning the presidency contradicts the claim of marginality.
option_explanations.C: Expanding liberal programs under Democratic majorities shows which ideology was dominant.
option_explanations.D: A decade of Democratic congressional control is consistent with conservatism being a minority outlook.

items.stem: The conservative coalition that elected Ronald Reagan in 1980 united which of the following groups?
options: (A) labor unions, civil rights organizations, and environmental activists
(B) isolationists, pacifists, and socialists
(C) supporters of expanded federal welfare programs
(D) economic conservatives, evangelicals, and anti-communists
items.explanation: Reagan's New Right coalition combined three strands: economic conservatives who wanted lower taxes and less regulation, evangelical Christians mobilized around social issues like abortion and school prayer, and anti-communists who favored a military buildup. Together they gave conservatism a mass base it had lacked in the 1960s.

option_explanations.A: Labor unions, civil rights groups, and environmentalists were core Democratic constituencies, not Reagan's coalition.
option_explanations.B: Reagan was a Cold War hawk, not an isolationist or pacifist, and socialists opposed him.
option_explanations.C: Reagan campaigned against the expansion of federal welfare programs, declaring government was the problem.
option_explanations.D: Correct. These three groups formed the backbone of the Reagan coalition.

items.stem: The founding of the Moral Majority is best understood as
items.stimulus: In 1973 the Supreme Court decided Roe v. Wade. In 1979, evangelical leaders founded the Moral Majority.
options: (A) evangelical Christians organizing politically around abortion
(B) a labor union formed to protect American factory jobs
(C) an environmental campaign against industrial pollution
(D) a bipartisan campaign to reduce the rapidly growing federal deficit
items.explanation: The Moral Majority, founded by Reverend Jerry Falwell in 1979, registered evangelical voters and lobbied against abortion, for school prayer, and for traditional family values. It turned evangelical churches, previously politically quiet, into a powerful force in the conservative coalition.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Abortion and related social issues were the Moral Majority's organizing causes.
option_explanations.B: The Moral Majority was a religious-political organization, not a labor union.
option_explanations.C: Environmental issues were not part of the Moral Majority's agenda.
option_explanations.D: Deficit reduction was an economic-conservative goal; the Moral Majority focused on social and moral issues.

items.stem: Madison's reference to a 'seventh pillar' meant that
items.stimulus: "There seems to be no question that the issue there will add a seventh pillar, as the phrase now is, to the Federal Temple." Source: James Madison, letter to George Washington, 1788.
options: (A) seven amendments had been added to the Constitution by 1788
(B) the Constitution had created seven separate and equal branches of government
(C) seven states had voted to reject the Constitution entirely
(D) New Hampshire would be the seventh state to ratify the Constitution
items.explanation: Supporters of the Constitution celebrated each ratifying state as a 'pillar' holding up the 'Federal Temple.' When Madison wrote in early 1788, six states had ratified, and he expected New Hampshire's convention to add the seventh. (In the event, Maryland and South Carolina ratified first, making New Hampshire the ninth state and the one that put the Constitution into effect.) The 'pillar' image counted states joining the new government.

option_explanations.A: No amendments had been added in 1788; the Bill of Rights would not be ratified until 1791.
option_explanations.B: The Constitution created three branches of government, not seven.
option_explanations.C: Madison was counting states joining the new government, not rejecting it.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Madison expected New Hampshire to become the seventh ratifying state, adding another 'pillar' to the Federal Temple.

items.stem: The Anti-Federalists' central objection to the Constitution was that it
options: (A) abolished slavery immediately throughout the states
(B) gave too much power to the states
(C) built a strong central government with no bill of rights
(D) banned the formation of political parties in the new republic
items.explanation: Anti-Federalists argued that the Constitution concentrated dangerous power in a distant national government and lacked explicit protections for individual liberty. Their pressure forced Federalists to promise a bill of rights, which was ratified in 1791 as the price of the Constitution's acceptance.

option_explanations.A: The Constitution protected slavery through compromises; it did not abolish it.
option_explanations.B: Anti-Federalists thought the states kept too little power, not too much.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Fear of centralized power plus the missing bill of rights was the core objection.
option_explanations.D: The Constitution says nothing about political parties, which emerged in the 1790s.

items.stem: The Anti-Federalist concern about centralized power reappeared most directly in
options: (A) the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions of 1798-1799
(B) the Missouri Compromise of 1820 and its limits on slavery
(C) the Monroe Doctrine of 1823
(D) the annexation of Texas in 1845
items.explanation: When the Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts, Jefferson and Madison answered with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, arguing that states could judge federal overreach. The resolutions revived the Anti-Federalist argument that concentrated national power threatened liberty.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The resolutions carried the Anti-Federalist states'-rights argument into the 1790s.
option_explanations.B: The Missouri Compromise concerned slavery's geographic limits, not federal power generally.
option_explanations.C: The Monroe Doctrine addressed foreign policy in the Americas.
option_explanations.D: Texas annexation was about expansion and slavery, not the Anti-Federalist critique.

items.stem: In this preamble, Parliament stated that the purpose of the Sugar Act was to
items.stimulus: "Whereas it is expedient that new provisions and regulations should be established for improving the revenue of this kingdom..." Source: Preamble to the Sugar Act, passed by Parliament, 1764.
options: (A) grant the colonies independence
(B) punish only French smugglers
(C) end the transatlantic slave trade
(D) raise revenue for Great Britain
items.explanation: The preamble states the purpose openly: improving the revenue of the kingdom. After the expensive Seven Years' War, Parliament wanted the colonies to contribute to imperial costs, and the Sugar Act was the first major law designed to do so.

option_explanations.A: Parliament was tightening control over the colonies, not granting independence.
option_explanations.B: The act applied broadly to colonial trade; it was not aimed only at French smugglers.
option_explanations.C: The Sugar Act concerned duties on goods such as sugar and molasses, not the slave trade.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Raising revenue is the stated purpose in the preamble itself.

items.stem: The Sugar Act angered colonists more than earlier British trade laws primarily because it
options: (A) was never actually enforced by British customs officials at all
(B) was openly designed to raise revenue from the colonies
(C) applied only to trade with France
(D) freed enslaved people throughout the colonies
items.explanation: Earlier measures like the Navigation Acts regulated trade, which colonists accepted as part of the empire. The Sugar Act of 1764 was different: its preamble stated openly that it would raise revenue for Britain. Colonists read it as taxation imposed by a Parliament in which they had no representatives.

option_explanations.A: The Sugar Act was enforced, unlike the earlier Molasses Act of 1733. Stricter enforcement was part of why colonists noticed and resented it.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The revenue purpose, stated openly in the act, is what made it a tax in colonial eyes.
option_explanations.C: The act applied broadly to colonial trade, not only to France.
option_explanations.D: The Sugar Act had nothing to do with slavery; it concerned duties on goods such as sugar and molasses.

items.stem: The Sugar Act of 1764 was part of Parliament's effort to
items.stimulus: Britain's national debt roughly doubled during the Seven Years' War (1756-1763). After the war, Parliament sought new income from the American colonies.
options: (A) make the colonies help pay for war and empire
(B) reward the colonies for their loyalty during the war
(C) encourage colonial manufacturing
(D) reduce the size of the British navy after the war
items.explanation: Victory in the Seven Years' War left Britain with enormous debts and a vast new North American territory to administer and defend. Ministers like George Grenville concluded that the colonies, which had benefited from British protection, should contribute revenue. The Sugar Act was the first in a series of revenue measures built on that logic.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Paying down war debt and funding imperial administration were the driving motives.
option_explanations.B: Parliament was not rewarding the colonies; it was demanding money from them, which is why the measures provoked resistance.
option_explanations.C: British policy aimed to keep manufacturing in Britain, not encourage it in the colonies.
option_explanations.D: Parliament maintained and even expanded its military presence in North America after the war.

items.stem: All of the following helped produce the broad American prosperity of the early 1960s EXCEPT
options: (A) strong labor unions that supported high wages
(B) federal programs that expanded homeownership
(C) the stock market crash of 1929
(D) regulations that stabilized the banking system
items.explanation: Postwar prosperity rested on New Deal-era foundations: unions that kept wages high, the GI Bill and federal housing programs that built the suburbs, and banking reforms that prevented the panics of the past. The 1929 crash caused the Great Depression; it did not produce the prosperity of the 1960s.

option_explanations.A: Unions covered about a third of workers in the 1950s and helped keep factory wages high enough to support mass consumption.
option_explanations.B: Federal housing policy, including VA and FHA loans, made homeownership possible for millions of families.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 1929 crash destroyed prosperity; it did not create it.
option_explanations.D: New Deal banking reforms, including deposit insurance, gave the financial system a stability it had lacked in the 1920s.

items.stem: The rapid growth of suburbs after 1945 was most directly facilitated by
options: (A) a sharp decline in automobile ownership after the war
(B) new highways and federal home-loan programs
(C) the demolition of suburban housing by urban renewal programs
(D) falling birth rates after the baby boom
items.explanation: The GI Bill gave veterans low-cost home loans, the Federal Housing Administration insured mortgages, and the Interstate Highway Act of 1956 built highways that made commuting practical. Together, cheap mortgages and new roads let millions of families buy single-family homes outside the cities.

option_explanations.A: Automobile ownership rose sharply after the war; the car made suburban living possible, not decline.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Federal loans plus highways were the two engines of suburbanization.
option_explanations.C: Urban renewal demolished inner-city neighborhoods, not suburbs, and often displaced the poor.
option_explanations.D: Birth rates rose during the baby boom, increasing the demand for suburban family homes.

items.stem: President Johnson's War on Poverty is best understood as a response to
items.stimulus: In 1964, more than 17 percent of Americans lived below the official poverty line, even as the overall economy prospered and income inequality stood near historic lows.
options: (A) poverty persisting amid national affluence
(B) the economic crisis of the Great Depression in the 1930s
(C) the energy shortages of the 1970s
(D) the decline of American manufacturing in the 1970s
items.explanation: Johnson launched the War on Poverty, with programs like Head Start, Job Corps, and expanded Social Security, precisely because millions remained poor in the richest nation on earth. The contrast between general prosperity and persistent poverty, documented in works like Michael Harrington's The Other America (1962), made poverty a national political issue.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Poverty amid affluence was the problem the Great Society set out to solve.
option_explanations.B: The Great Depression had ended twenty years earlier; the 1960s economy was booming.
option_explanations.C: The energy shortages came in 1973 and 1979, after Johnson left office.
option_explanations.D: Large-scale deindustrialization came later, in the 1970s and 1980s.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

stimulus_text.attribution: Paraphrased from Oswald Garrison Villard, John Brown 1800-1859: A Biography Fifty Years After (1910), the first full scholarly biography of Brown.
stimulus_text.text: Villard presented John Brown as a deeply committed antislavery militant rather than a madman. He argued that Brown's raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry in 1859 should be judged against the violence of slavery itself: Brown used force because he believed slavery was a state of war against Black people, and he had concluded that moral appeals alone would never end it.

parts: A. Briefly explain one claim Villard makes about John Brown.
B. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from the period 1848 to 1860 that supports Villard's interpretation of Brown.
C. Briefly explain one piece of evidence from the period 1848 to 1860 that challenges Villard's interpretation of Brown.

exemplar.A: Villard claims that Brown was a principled antislavery militant, not a fanatic, and that his violence should be measured against the violence of slavery itself.
exemplar.B: Brown's actions in 'Bleeding Kansas,' where he led antislavery settlers in armed conflict with proslavery forces, support Villard's view that Brown was a committed militant acting on antislavery principle rather than impulse.
exemplar.C: The failure of enslaved people to rise up during the Harpers Ferry raid challenges Villard's interpretation, because it suggests Brown badly misread the situation; Abraham Lincoln likewise judged the raid 'absurd' in an 1860 speech, arguing that even the enslaved saw it could not succeed.

stimulus_text.attribution: Paraphrased from the Fugitive Slave Act, passed by Congress as part of the Compromise of 1850.
stimulus_text.text: The law required federal marshals to arrest alleged fugitives and bring them before special commissioners. The accused person was denied a jury trial and was not permitted to testify in the hearing. Commissioners received a larger fee when they ruled that the accused person was a fugitive than when they ruled the person was free.

parts: A. Briefly explain one way the law strengthened the power of slaveholders.
B. Briefly explain one Northern reaction to the law.
C. Briefly explain how the law affected the sectional crisis of the 1850s.

exemplar.A: The law gave slaveholders a federal enforcement mechanism: marshals were required to help capture alleged fugitives, and commissioners had a financial incentive to rule in the slaveholder's favor.
exemplar.B: Many Northerners who had been indifferent to abolition were outraged at being legally required to help catch fugitives, and several Northern states passed personal-liberty laws to obstruct enforcement of the act.
exemplar.C: The law deepened sectional distrust by forcing Northerners to participate in slavery, pushing previously moderate Northerners toward antislavery politics and into the new Republican Party.

stimulus_text.attribution: Image 1: Jacob Riis, c.1890, public domain via Wikimedia Commons (Library of Congress). Image 2: CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.
stimulus_text.text: Image 1: 'Lodgers in a crowded Bayard Street tenement,' photograph by Jacob Riis, New York City, c.1890. The image shows men crowded together sleeping in a single small tenement room, with a stove and their belongings piled around them. Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/c2/Jacob_Riis%2C_Lodgers_in_a_Crowded_Bayard_Street_Tenement.jpg (Jacob Riis, c.1890; public domain via Wikimedia Commons.) Image 2: bedroom of Cornelius Vanderbilt II at The Breakers mansion, Newport, Rhode Island (mansion completed 1895). The image shows the spacious, richly furnished bedroom of a Gilded Age industrialist. Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/92/Cornelius_Bedroom_Breakers.JPG (CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons.)

parts: A. Briefly describe one contrast between the two images.
B. Briefly explain one development from 1865 to 1920 that produced the living conditions shown in Image 1.
C. Briefly explain one response to the conditions shown in Image 1 during the same period.

exemplar.A: Image 1 shows men crowded together sleeping in a single small tenement room, while Image 2 shows a Gilded Age industrialist's spacious, elegant bedroom; the pair makes visible the gap between tenement poverty and Gilded Age wealth.
exemplar.B: Rapid industrialization drew thousands of immigrant and rural workers into cities, where low wages and a severe shortage of affordable housing forced families into crowded, unsanitary tenements.
exemplar.C: Settlement-house workers such as Jane Addams at Hull House, opened in Chicago in 1889, provided services to tenement neighborhoods, while Progressive reformers campaigned for tenement inspections and housing regulations.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the migration of African Americans out of the South transformed American society from 1920 to 1970.

documents.text: Share of the Black population living in the South, by census year: 1900: about 90% | 1930: about 79% | 1960: about 60% | 1970: about 53%. Source: U.S. Census Bureau, decennial censuses.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: the federal census. Purpose: count and locate the population. The figures establish the scale and timing of the migration but do not explain why people moved.

documents.text: Paraphrased from an editorial in the Chicago Defender, a leading Black newspaper: The paper urged Black Southerners to leave the South for Northern cities, where factories were hiring at higher wages and where, the editors wrote, a Black man could vote and send his children to better schools.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: a Northern Black newspaper. Purpose: encourage migration, which also sold newspapers. Audience: Black Southerners. The paper had an interest in promoting the movement it championed.

documents.text: Paraphrased from a letter by a Black woman in Louisiana to the Chicago Defender: She wrote that she earned very low wages, that her family faced constant mistreatment, and asked whether the paper could help her find work and a place to live in Chicago.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: a prospective migrant writing firsthand. Purpose: seek practical help. The letter shows the push factors of low wages and mistreatment in a migrant's own voice.

documents.text: "...there shall be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries or government because of race, creed, color, or national origin..." Source: Executive Order 8802, issued by President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: the president. Historical situation: issued days before A. Philip Randolph's planned March on Washington protesting job discrimination. Purpose: head off the march and staff defense plants. Shows migration-era pressure producing federal action.

documents.text: Net Black migration by state, 1940-1970: Largest net gains: Illinois, New York, California, Michigan, Pennsylvania. Largest net losses: Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, South Carolina, Louisiana. Source: U.S. Census Bureau.
documents.sourcing_note: POV: the federal census. The figures map the Second Great Migration: out of the Deep South and into Northern and Western industrial states. Pairs with Document 1 to show change over time.

documents.text: [Image: photograph by Russell Lee, Farm Security Administration, Chicago, April 1941 (public domain, Library of Congress). The photograph shows young Black Chicagoans in Easter finery posing on an automobile on the city's South Side.] Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ac/No_Known_Restrictions_Easter_morning_on_the_Southside_of_Chicago%2C_Illinois_by_Russell_Lee%2C_1941_%28LOC%29_%28290626707%29.jpg (Russell Lee, 1941; public domain via Wikimedia Commons; Library of Congress FSA-OWI Collection.)
documents.sourcing_note: POV: a federal photographer documenting American life. Purpose: record the migration for the government. A visual complement to the census numbers: migration as lived human experience.

documents.text: [Image: Home Owners' Loan Corporation 'residential security' map of Chicago, late 1930s (public domain, federal government). Neighborhoods are graded A through D; Black neighborhoods on the South and West Sides are outlined in red and marked 'hazardous' for mortgage lending.] Image: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e2/Holc-chicago.jpg (Home Owners' Loan Corporation; public domain dedication (CC0) via Wikimedia Commons.)
documents.sourcing_note: POV: a federal housing agency. Purpose: guide private lending decisions. The map shows that Northern cities, while offering jobs, used official policy to segregate Black migrants. It is strong evidence for the limits of the transformation the migration produced.

section_2b.directions: Section II, Part B — Long Essay: 1 question, 40 minutes. Develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, and support your argument with specific and relevant examples. This part counts for 15 percent of the exam score. Total exam time: 3 hours 15 minutes.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the Mexican-American War led to the American Civil War in the period 1844 to 1860.
leq.guidance: The war between the United States and Mexico (1846-1848) ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which transferred California and the vast Southwest to the United States. Within a few years, Americans were fighting - in Congress, in Kansas, and finally on battlefields - over whether slavery would be permitted in the new territory. Suggested areas: Political developments, such as the Wilmot Proviso, the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and the formation of the Republican Party; Economic developments, such as the expansion of plantation slavery and debates over free versus enslaved labor in the West; Social and ideological developments, such as the growth of abolitionism, Southern defenses of slavery, and the idea of popular sovereignty
